sportboot-see-elwis-184.explanation: The signs shown mark a prohibited area, i.e. an area closed to shipping in general or to certain types of vessel. Such signs must be strictly observed, since entering a prohibited area can often involve considerable danger (e.g. military use, unexploded ordnance, nature conservation). The exact boundaries and any exceptions are given in the associated official notice.

sportboot-see-elwis-190.question: What does the following buoy mean?

options.a: Marking of the port side of a fairway.
options.b: Marking the middle of shipping channels.
options.c: Marking of an anchorage.
options.d: Marking of isolated dangers.

sportboot-see-elwis-190.explanation: This buoy (vertically striped red and white, with a spherical topmark) marks, under the IALA system, the middle of a shipping channel or fairway. It indicates that there is sufficient water on both sides and that the buoy should be passed close by, straddling it. It is clearly distinguished from the lateral red or green buoys by its colour and topmark.

sportboot-see-elwis-191.question: What does the following sign mean?

options.a: The starboard side of the fairway.
options.b: The port side of the fairway.
options.c: The middle of a shipping route.
options.d: Marking of obstructions.

sportboot-see-elwis-191.explanation: The sign shown marks the starboard side of the fairway (green colour, conical topmark), as seen by a vessel coming from seaward, under the IALA Region A buoyage system used on German seaward waterways. For safe navigation, this buoy must be kept to starboard when entering from seaward. Colour, shape, and topmark are the decisive identifying features.

sportboot-see-elwis-192.question: What does the following sign mean?

options.a: Marking of an obstruction in the wadden fairway.
options.b: The port side of the fairway.
options.c: The middle of a wadden fairway.
options.d: The starboard side of the fairway.

sportboot-see-elwis-192.explanation: The sign shown marks the port side of the fairway (red colour, cylindrical topmark), as seen by a vessel coming from seaward. When entering from seaward, this buoy must therefore be kept to port, and correspondingly to starboard when leaving. This colour coding under the IALA Region A system is one of the most fundamental rules of coastal navigation.

sportboot-see-elwis-193.question: What does the following buoy/sign mean?

options.a: The middle of a shipping route.
options.b: Marking of obstructions.
options.c: The port side of the fairway.
options.d: The starboard side of the fairway.

sportboot-see-elwis-193.explanation: This sign also marks the starboard side of the fairway, recognizable by its green colour and conical topmark, as seen by a vessel entering from seaward. Colour and topmark shape complement each other so that the side can be identified unambiguously even in poor visibility or at night, thanks to the corresponding green light.

sportboot-see-elwis-194.question: What does the following buoy/sign mean?

options.a: Marking of an obstruction in the wadden fairway.
options.b: The middle of a wadden fairway.
options.c: The starboard side of the fairway.
options.d: The port side of the fairway.

sportboot-see-elwis-194.explanation: This sign marks the port side of the fairway, recognizable by its red colour and cylindrical (can-shaped) topmark, as seen by a vessel entering from seaward. At night this side is additionally marked by a red light, so the identification remains unambiguous even in darkness.

sportboot-see-elwis-195.question: What does the following buoy mean?

options.a: Port side of the through fairway.
options.b: Starboard side of the through fairway / port side of the branching or joining fairway.
options.c: Starboard side of the through fairway.
options.d: Port side of the through fairway / starboard side of the branching or joining fairway.

sportboot-see-elwis-195.explanation: This buoy marks a preferred fairway side at a fork in the fairway: it simultaneously indicates the starboard side of the main through fairway and the port side of a branching or joining secondary fairway. Such preferred-channel marks, combining two colour bands, carry two meanings depending on which branch of the fairway you are following, and are typical at junctions in the buoyage system.

sportboot-see-elwis-196.question: What does the following buoy mean?

options.a: Starboard side of the through fairway, port side of the branching or joining fairway.
options.b: Port side of the through fairway.
options.c: Starboard side of the through fairway.
options.d: Port side of the through fairway, starboard side of the branching or joining fairway.

sportboot-see-elwis-196.explanation: This buoy shows the reverse combination: it marks the port side of the main through fairway and, at the same time, the starboard side of a branching or joining fairway. Such preferred-channel marks with two colour bands (a dominant base colour plus a narrow band of the opposite colour) are needed at fairway junctions to give clear orientation for both directions of traffic.

sportboot-see-elwis-200.question: What does the following sign mean?

options.a: Marking of a general danger area, south quadrant.
options.b: Marking of a general danger area, north quadrant.
options.c: Marking of a general danger area, east quadrant.
options.d: Marking of a general danger area, west quadrant.

sportboot-see-elwis-200.explanation: This sign is a cardinal mark of the IALA system, whose black double-cone topmarks both point upward. This identifies the north quadrant of a general danger area, which must accordingly be passed to the north to safely avoid the hazard. The orientation of the cones in the topmark is the decisive identifying feature of all cardinal marks.

sportboot-see-elwis-201.question: What does the following sign mean?

options.a: Marking of a general danger area, west quadrant.
options.b: Marking of a general danger area, north quadrant.
options.c: Marking of a general danger area, south quadrant.
options.d: Marking of a general danger area, east quadrant.

sportboot-see-elwis-201.explanation: On this cardinal mark, the two black cones in the topmark point away from each other (the upper one up, the lower one down). This identifies the east quadrant of a general danger area, which must accordingly be passed to the east. This cone arrangement is clearly distinct from the north, south, and west cardinal marks.

sportboot-see-elwis-202.question: What does the following sign mean?

options.a: Marking of a general danger area, north quadrant.
options.b: Marking of a general danger area, east quadrant.
options.c: Marking of a general danger area, south quadrant.
options.d: Marking of a general danger area, west quadrant.

sportboot-see-elwis-202.explanation: On this cardinal mark, both black cones in the topmark point downward. This identifies the south quadrant of a general danger area, which must accordingly be passed to the south. This mark is also typically painted yellow over black, with the yellow band above the black, confirming it as the south cardinal mark.

sportboot-see-elwis-203.question: What does the following sign mean?

options.a: Marking of a general danger area, east quadrant.
options.b: Marking of a general danger area, north quadrant.
options.c: Marking of a general danger area, west quadrant.
options.d: Marking of a general danger area, south quadrant.

sportboot-see-elwis-203.explanation: On this cardinal mark, the two black cones in the topmark point toward each other, base to base, forming an hourglass shape. This identifies the west quadrant of a general danger area, which must accordingly be passed to the west. This characteristic hourglass shape is clearly distinct from the arrangements of the other three cardinal marks.

sportboot-see-elwis-204.question: What does the light of a lit buoy with the following characteristic mean?

options.a: Marking of a general danger area, to be passed to the east.
options.b: Marking of a general danger area, to be passed to the north.
options.c: Marking of a general danger area, to be passed to the west.
options.d: Marking of a general danger area, to be passed to the south.

sportboot-see-elwis-204.explanation: The described light characteristic is typical for the north cardinal mark: a continuous quick or very quick flashing light without a fixed group rhythm. It indicates that the danger lies in the north quadrant and must be passed to the north in order to stay safely clear of the hazard.

sportboot-see-elwis-205.question: What does the light of a lit buoy with the following characteristic mean?

options.a: Marking of a general danger area, to be passed to the south.
options.b: Marking of a general danger area, to be passed to the east.
options.c: Marking of a general danger area, to be passed to the north.
options.d: Marking of a general danger area, to be passed to the west.

sportboot-see-elwis-205.explanation: The light characteristic described, a group of three flashes (Q(3) or VQ(3)), is the characteristic signature of the east cardinal mark. A common memory aid ties it to a clock face: three flashes, like "3 o'clock", stands for east. The danger therefore lies in the east quadrant and must be passed to the east.

sportboot-see-elwis-206.question: What does the light of a lit buoy with the following characteristic mean?

options.a: Marking of a general danger area, east quadrant.
options.b: Marking of a general danger area, west quadrant.
options.c: Marking of a general danger area, south quadrant.
options.d: Marking of a general danger area, north quadrant.

sportboot-see-elwis-206.explanation: The light characteristic described, a group of six flashes followed by one long flash (Q(6)+LFl or VQ(6)+LFl), is the characteristic signature of the south cardinal mark. The six flashes symbolically represent "6 o'clock" on a clock face, and the additional long flash serves as a clear distinguishing feature from other characteristics. The danger accordingly lies in the south quadrant.

sportboot-see-elwis-207.question: What does the light of a lit buoy with the following characteristic mean?

options.a: Marking of a general danger area, north quadrant; it must be passed to the north.
options.b: Marking of a general danger area, south quadrant; it must be passed to the south.
options.c: Marking of a general danger area, east quadrant; it must be passed to the east.
options.d: Marking of a general danger area, west quadrant; it must be passed to the west.

sportboot-see-elwis-207.explanation: The light characteristic described, a group of nine flashes (Q(9) or VQ(9)), is the characteristic signature of the west cardinal mark - the nine flashes symbolically represent "9 o'clock". The danger therefore lies in the west quadrant and must accordingly be passed to the west, in order to stay safely clear of the hazard.

sportboot-see-elwis-208.question: What does one of the following signs mark and what conduct does it require?

options.a: An isolated danger that may be passed on all sides.
options.b: The north quadrant of a general danger area, which must be passed to the north.
options.c: The west quadrant of a general danger area, which must be passed to the west.
options.d: The south quadrant of a general danger area, which must be passed to the south.

sportboot-see-elwis-208.explanation: The sign shown is an isolated danger mark (black-red-black with two black spheres, one above the other, as topmark). It marks a limited, isolated danger (e.g. a wreck) that, unlike with cardinal marks, may be passed on any side at a safe distance. It must therefore be treated fundamentally differently from the north, east, south, and west cardinal marks.

sportboot-see-elwis-209.question: What does the light of a lit buoy with the following characteristic mean: Fl.(2)?

options.a: An isolated danger that may be passed on all sides.
options.b: South quadrant of a general danger area, which must be passed to the south.
options.c: North quadrant of a general danger area, which must be passed to the north.
options.d: West quadrant of a general danger area, which must be passed to the west.

sportboot-see-elwis-209.explanation: The light characteristic Fl.(2), a group of two flashes, is the characteristic signature of an isolated danger mark. This buoy may be passed on any side, as long as a sufficient safety margin is kept, since unlike cardinal marks it does not prescribe a direction from which the danger must be approached.

sportboot-see-elwis-210.question: What is meant by a "leading light" (Leitfeuer)?

options.a: Upper and lower lights with different colour sectors.
options.b: A directional sector light indicating a change of course in the fairway.
options.c: A sector light that marks a fairway.
options.d: Upper and lower lights that must be brought into line (in transit).

sportboot-see-elwis-210.explanation: A leading light (Leitfeuer) is a sector light that marks a fairway using differently coloured light sectors, typically white for the safe channel area and red and green for the danger areas to either side. The navigator holds course as long as the white sector is visible and knows, on switching to the red or green sector, that they are leaving the safe area. It must be clearly distinguished from a range light (Richtfeuer), which consists of two lights that must be brought into transit.

sportboot-see-elwis-212.question: What is meant by a "range light" (Richtfeuer)?

options.a: A sector light that marks a fairway.
options.b: Upper and lower lights with different colour sectors.
options.c: Upper and lower lights that must be brought into line (in transit).
options.d: A directional sector light indicating a change of course in the fairway.

sportboot-see-elwis-212.explanation: A range light (Richtfeuer) consists of an upper and a lower light erected on a common leading line, which the navigator must bring into transit (line up) in order to stay safely within the fairway. If the two lights appear to diverge, the vessel is off to one side of the intended track. It differs from a sector light (leading light) in that it relies on the transit principle rather than colour sectors.

sportboot-see-elwis-213.question: What is meant by a "cross light" (Quermarkenfeuer)?

options.a: A sector light that marks a fairway.
options.b: Upper and lower lights that must be brought into line (in transit).
options.c: A directional sector light indicating a change of course in the fairway.
options.d: Upper and lower lights with different colour sectors.

sportboot-see-elwis-213.explanation: A cross light (Quermarkenfeuer) is a sector light that indicates an upcoming change of course in the fairway, by changing colour or characteristic at the relevant point. This allows the navigator to recognize in good time that the fairway bends at that position and that course must be adjusted. It differs functionally from a leading light, which marks a straight, safe course over a longer stretch.

sportboot-see-elwis-232.question: What information do the Notices to Mariners (NfS) and the Announcements for Seafarers (BfS) contain?

options.a: They contain all changes regarding buoyage, lights, wrecks, shoals, and other changes to the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung.
options.b: They contain all changes regarding buoyage, lights, wrecks, shoals, and other meteorological information affecting shipping.
options.c: They contain all changes regarding buoyage, lights, wrecks, and current water levels.
options.d: They contain all changes regarding buoyage, lights, wrecks, shoals, and other measures and events affecting shipping.

sportboot-see-elwis-232.explanation: The Notices to Mariners (NfS) and the Announcements for Seafarers (BfS) contain all changes regarding buoyage, lights, wrecks, and shoals, as well as other measures and events affecting shipping (e.g. construction work, closures, exercise areas). They are used to continuously correct charts, lists of lights, and sailing directions, and to inform the navigator of current changes in the area of operation. Weather forecasts or water levels are not their main subject.

sportboot-see-elwis-238.question: Where does one find the navigationally important descriptions of shipping marks, their lighting, and information on signal stations?

options.a: List of Lights, Sailing Directions, nautical charts.
options.b: List of Lights, Sailing Directions, Bridge and Chart Room Handbook.
options.c: List of Lights, Sailing Directions, Collision Regulations.
options.d: List of Lights, Sailing Directions, tidal atlas.

sportboot-see-elwis-238.explanation: The important navigational descriptions of shipping marks, their lighting, and signal stations are found in the List of Lights, the Sailing Directions, and the nautical charts themselves. These three sources complement one another: the chart shows position and symbol, the List of Lights gives the exact light characteristic and range, and the Sailing Directions describe additional details in text form. Together they form the basis for safe nautical planning.

sportboot-see-elwis-271.question: How, based on the seaman's duty of care, should one adjust one's navigation in the fairway in reduced visibility if the vessel lacks the technical equipment, in particular for detecting other vessels?

options.a: Stop immediately and anchor; if this is not possible, proceed cautiously and, if possible, keep in the wake of a vessel ahead.
options.b: Proceed prudently but at a good pace, so as not to obstruct the rest of the traffic. On hearing another vessel's fog signal, stop and wait, continuously taking soundings.
options.c: Keep as far to the right as possible in the fairway and make for the nearest harbour or berth. If in doubt, ask other vessels for their position and correct course.
options.d: Leave the fairway and, if possible, seek out a shallow-water area and anchor. If this is not possible, keep as far to the right as possible in the fairway.

sportboot-see-elwis-271.explanation: If a vessel lacks the technical equipment to detect other vessels (e.g. radar) in reduced visibility, the seaman's duty of care requires leaving the fairway and, if possible, seeking out a shallow-water area outside the fairway to anchor there, in order to avoid any risk of collision with traffic in the fairway. If this is not possible, one must keep as far to the right as possible within the fairway (i.e. on one's own starboard side), so as to stay out of the way of oncoming traffic as much as possible and remain predictable.

sportboot-see-elwis-75.question: Which pleasure craft are exempt from the requirement to hold a licence on seaward waterways?

options.a: Pleasure craft that are either anchored, made fast ashore, or aground.
options.b: Pleasure craft without a propulsion engine, or those with a maximum permitted power output of 11.03 kilowatts (15 hp) using an internal combustion engine, or 7.5 kilowatts using an electric motor in continuous duty (S1) or less.
options.c: Sailing pleasure craft with a hull length under 20 m and those whose propulsion engine is not being used.
options.d: Pleasure craft with a propulsion engine of greater power output than 11.03 kilowatts (15 hp) using an internal combustion engine, or 7.5 kilowatts using an electric motor in continuous duty (S1).

sportboot-see-elwis-75.explanation: Exempt from the licensing requirement on seaward waterways are pleasure craft without a propulsion engine, and pleasure craft with an engine up to a maximum power output of 11.03 kilowatts (15 hp) for internal combustion engines, or 7.5 kilowatts for electric motors in continuous duty (S1). This power threshold marks the point above which a pleasure craft is classified as potentially more hazardous to other traffic, making an official certificate of competence necessary. Being at anchor or aground, by contrast, does not remove the underlying licensing requirement that applies once the vessel gets underway.

sportboot-see-elwis-77.question: What is meant by the "seaman's duty of care"?

options.a: The obligation to observe the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung (SeeSchStrO), the Collision Regulations (KVR), the basic rules of conduct in traffic, and the avoiding rules including the manoeuvre of last resort.
options.b: The obligation to observe the precautions of the Collision Regulations (KVR), the basic rules of conduct in traffic, and the avoiding rules including the manoeuvre of last resort.
options.c: The obligation to observe the precautions and safety rules of the traffic regulations and the basic rules of conduct in traffic.
options.d: The obligation to observe precautions beyond the traffic regulations that ordinary seamanship practice or the special circumstances of the case require.

sportboot-see-elwis-77.explanation: The seaman's duty of care means the obligation to observe, beyond the written traffic regulations, all precautions that ordinary seamanship practice or the particular circumstances of the case require. It recognizes that no set of rules can conclusively cover every conceivable situation at sea, and therefore demands additional prudent, forward-looking conduct from the vessel's skipper. This duty is explicitly anchored in the Collision Regulations and supplements, rather than replaces, the specific right-of-way and avoiding rules.

sportboot-see-elwis-79.question: What is meant by the "manoeuvre of last resort"?

options.a: The avoiding manoeuvre of the stand-on vessel or the give-way vessel.
options.b: The avoiding manoeuvre of the stand-on vessel.
options.c: The avoiding manoeuvre of the stand-on vessel and the give-way vessel.
options.d: The avoiding manoeuvre of the give-way vessel.

sportboot-see-elwis-79.explanation: The "manoeuvre of last resort" refers to the avoiding action taken by the stand-on vessel, i.e. the vessel that actually has right of way. It applies when the give-way vessel fails to fulfil its obligation in time and a collision can no longer be reliably avoided by that vessel's action alone. In that case, the stand-on vessel itself must also take suitable action to avoid the collision, even though it otherwise has priority.

sportboot-see-elwis-80.question: When must the "maneuver of last resort" be carried out?

options.a: It must be carried out when a collision can no longer be avoided by the stand-on vessel's maneuvers alone.
options.b: It must be carried out when a collision can no longer be avoided by the give-way vessel's maneuvers alone.
options.c: It must be carried out shortly before the collision, if a collision can otherwise no longer be avoided by the stand-on vessel's maneuvers alone.
options.d: It must be carried out at the last moment by everyone if a collision can otherwise no longer be avoided.

sportboot-see-elwis-80.explanation: The "maneuver of last resort" is an emergency action taken only by the give-way vessel, when its own avoiding action alone can no longer prevent a collision. The stand-on vessel, by contrast, must initially keep her course and speed and may only intervene once it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not reacting appropriately.

sportboot-see-elwis-82.question: When is a vessel "not under command"?

options.a: When it is restricted by the nature of its work and therefore cannot maneuver as required and consequently cannot give way to another vessel.
options.b: When, owing to some exceptional circumstance, e.g. failure of the steering gear or engine, it is unable to maneuver as required and therefore cannot give way to another vessel.
options.c: When it is severely restricted by its draught in relation to the available depth and width of navigable water and is therefore unable to deviate from its course.
options.d: When it is fishing with nets, lines, trawls or other fishing gear that restricts its maneuverability.

sportboot-see-elwis-82.explanation: "Not under command" means that a vessel is, owing to an exceptional circumstance such as steering or engine failure, temporarily unable to maneuver as required. It shows two red all-round lights in a vertical line (or two black balls by day) and enjoys special protection from other vessels because it cannot give way itself.

sportboot-see-elwis-83.question: When is a vessel "restricted in her ability to maneuver"?

options.a: When it is fishing with nets, lines, trawls or other fishing gear that restricts its maneuverability.
options.b: When it is severely restricted by its draught in relation to the available depth and width of navigable water and is therefore unable to deviate from its course.
options.c: When it is restricted by the nature of its work and therefore cannot maneuver as required and consequently cannot give way to another vessel.
options.d: When, owing to some exceptional circumstance, e.g. failure of the steering gear or engine, it is unable to maneuver as required and therefore cannot give way to another vessel.

sportboot-see-elwis-83.explanation: A vessel is "restricted in her ability to maneuver" when the nature of its work (e.g. dredging, towing, fishing with nets, transferring a pilot) restricts its maneuverability, so it cannot give way as a normally maneuvering vessel could. This differs from "not under command", which presupposes a technical failure.

sportboot-see-elwis-119.question: Which vessel gives, in restricted visibility, immediately following the signal: prolonged, short, short

options.a: A vessel not under command of less than 100 m in length.
options.b: A vessel being towed, or the last manned vessel of a tow, when underway.
options.c: A vessel of less than 100 m in length at anchor carrying dangerous cargo.
options.d: A power-driven vessel underway that has stopped her engines and has no way through the water.

sportboot-see-elwis-119.explanation: In restricted visibility, the towed vessel (or the last manned vessel of a tow) gives her own signal (prolonged, short, short) immediately after the towing vessel's signal (prolonged, prolonged, short), to announce her position and warn others of the overall length of the tow.

sportboot-see-elwis-136.question: How must a give-way vessel behave towards a stand-on vessel?

options.a: Speed must be reduced to the minimum necessary to maintain steerage way; when in doubt, the vessel must stop completely.
options.b: The avoiding action must be taken early, be substantial, and be clearly recognizable.
options.c: The maneuver of last resort must be carried out. Avoiding action must be taken in whatever way is most helpful to avoid a collision.
options.d: The course must be adjusted step by step as the stand-on vessel is approached, so that the other vessel's stern is safely cleared.

sportboot-see-elwis-136.explanation: The give-way vessel must take avoiding action as early as possible, and it must be substantial and clearly recognizable as such to the stand-on vessel and any observer. Small, hesitant course changes are not permitted, as they can cause misunderstanding and thereby increase the risk of collision.

sportboot-see-elwis-145.question: How must a power-driven vessel behave, in a risk of collision, in a one-way traffic lane of a traffic separation scheme towards another power-driven vessel crossing the lane and coming from starboard?

options.a: It must carry out the maneuver of last resort.
options.b: It must give way to the other vessel.
options.c: It must pay particular attention to the crossing vessel.
options.d: It must not impede the safe passage of the power-driven vessel.

sportboot-see-elwis-145.explanation: Within a traffic lane of a traffic separation scheme, the ordinary crossing rule between two power-driven vessels still applies: the vessel crossing from starboard is the stand-on vessel, and the other vessel must give way. Crossing a lane should be avoided where possible, but this does not change the basic starboard-has-right-of-way principle.

sportboot-see-elwis-181.question: What is the maximum speed that must not be exceeded, outside the fairway, within 500 m of the shore off places with recognizable swimming activity?

options.a: 4.3 knots.
options.b: 3.4 knots.
options.c: 4.8 knots.
options.d: 3.8 knots.

sportboot-see-elwis-181.explanation: Within 500 m of the shore off recognizable swimming areas outside the fairway, a maximum speed of 4.3 knots (about 8 km/h) must be observed, so that swimmers are not endangered by wash, suction, or the vessels themselves.

sportboot-see-elwis-229.question: Unless the North Sea Traffic Regulation (NordSBefV) expressly states otherwise, what is the maximum speed a power-driven vessel may travel in national parks in the North Sea area?

options.a: 10 knots speed over ground.
options.b: 12 knots over ground.
options.c: 12 knots speed through the water.
options.d: 10 knots speed through the water.

sportboot-see-elwis-229.explanation: In the North Sea national parks, unless the North Sea Traffic Regulation states otherwise, power-driven vessels are generally limited to 12 knots speed over ground, to protect the sensitive Wadden Sea habitat and the birds and animals that breed or rest there.

sportboot-see-elwis-241.question: What does the speed unit "knot" mean?

options.a: That is the number of nautical miles covered from noon to noon.
options.b: That is the number of nautical miles covered in one hour.
options.c: That is the number of nautical miles covered in one day.
options.d: That is the number of kilometers covered in one hour.

sportboot-see-elwis-241.explanation: A knot is the unit of speed used at sea and equals one nautical mile (1,852 m) per hour. The term derives historically from the knotted log-line that was paid out astern to measure a vessel's speed.

sportboot-see-elwis-260.question: What does the following symbol mean?

options.a: Current towards northwest; strength: 3 knots; tidal area.
options.b: Wind towards northwest; strength: Bft. 3; cloudless.
options.c: Current from northwest; strength: 3 knots; tidal area.
options.d: Wind from northwest; strength: Bft. 3; cloudless.

sportboot-see-elwis-260.explanation: On weather-chart wind symbols, the wind barb shows the direction the wind is blowing from, and the number of barbs/feathers indicates the wind strength in Beaufort; an unfilled (empty) sky circle indicates cloudless skies. Together the symbol reads: wind from the northwest, force Beaufort 3, cloudless sky.

sportboot-see-elwis-285.question: What does one of the following signals mean on a vessel?

options.a: Vessel in distress.
options.b: Vessel is restricted in her ability to maneuver.
options.c: Vessel carrying dangerous cargo.
options.d: Vessel at anchor of more than 100 m in length.

sportboot-see-elwis-285.explanation: The signal shown belongs to the internationally recognized distress signals (e.g. under COLREGs Annex IV: smoke signal, red parachute flare, or slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering outstretched arms). Such signals may only be used to indicate a vessel in immediate distress, and every vessel within sight is obliged to render assistance.

sportboot-see-elwis-4.question: How long does a short blast last?

options.a: Less than 4 seconds.
options.b: Less than 1 second.
options.c: About 2 seconds.
options.d: About 1 second.

sportboot-see-elwis-4.explanation: Under the internationally defined sound signals, a short blast lasts about one second. It is the basic building block of the maneuvering and warning signals (for example, one short blast means "I am altering my course to starboard").

sportboot-see-elwis-5.question: How long does a prolonged blast last?

options.a: About 1 - 2 seconds.
options.b: About 4 - 6 seconds.
options.c: About 2 - 6 seconds.
options.d: About 6 - 8 seconds.

sportboot-see-elwis-5.explanation: A prolonged blast lasts about 4 to 6 seconds and is used, among other things, as the fog signal of a power-driven vessel making way through the water (one prolonged blast every 2 minutes), as well as in various maneuvering and warning signals.

sportboot-see-elwis-73.question: Where do the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs) apply?

options.a: On the high seas and on all waters connected therewith and navigable by seagoing vessels.
options.b: On seagoing shipping routes and coastal German sea waters that are navigated by seagoing vessels.
options.c: On the high seas and the German seagoing shipping routes navigated by seagoing vessels.
options.d: On the high seas and the marginal seas navigable by seagoing vessels, except for traffic separation schemes.

sportboot-see-elwis-73.explanation: The COLREGs apply worldwide on the high seas and on all waters connected therewith that are navigable by seagoing vessels, regardless of national borders. On German seagoing shipping routes, the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung additionally applies, supplementing the COLREGs with specific rules.

sportboot-see-elwis-76.question: Who is responsible for complying with the traffic rules?

options.a: The vessel's skipper and their deputy.
options.b: The vessel's skipper or their deputy.
options.c: The vessel's skipper or any other person in charge.
options.d: The vessel's skipper and any other person in charge.

sportboot-see-elwis-76.explanation: Responsibility for complying with the traffic rules rests with the skipper or, if the skipper has handed over command, with their deputy - the responsibility therefore always lies with exactly one person, whoever is actually in command of the vessel at the time.

sportboot-see-elwis-78.question: What safety measures must the skipper take, as part of their duty of seamanlike care, before departure, for the protection and safety of the persons on board?

options.a: The skipper must inform the crew members and guests about the safety arrangements on board, instruct them in the use of the life-saving and fire-fighting equipment, and point out suitable measures against falling overboard, as well as the fact that permanently worn life jackets increase chances of survival in the water.
options.b: The skipper must inform the guests on board about the safety arrangements on board, instruct them in the use of the life-saving and fire-fighting equipment, and point out suitable measures against falling overboard, as well as the fact that permanently worn life jackets increase chances of survival in the water.
options.c: The skipper must instruct the crew members and guests to inform themselves about the safety arrangements on board, to look at the instructions for the life-saving and fire-fighting equipment, and to pay attention to suitable measures against falling overboard, as well as the fact that permanently worn life jackets increase chances of survival in the water.
options.d: The skipper must inform the responsible crew members about the safety arrangements on board, instruct them in the use of the life-saving and fire-fighting equipment, and point out suitable measures against falling overboard, as well as the fact that permanently worn life jackets increase chances of survival in the water.

sportboot-see-elwis-78.explanation: As part of the skipper's duty of seamanlike care, before departure they must inform everyone on board - crew and guests alike - about the safety arrangements, instruct them in using the life-saving and fire-fighting equipment, and point out suitable measures against falling overboard as well as the benefit of permanently worn life jackets. This duty protects everyone on board, regardless of their status.

sportboot-see-elwis-81.question: When is a vessel considered to be an overtaking vessel?

options.a: When it is in a direction of more than 22.5° abaft the beam of another vessel (sector of the sternlight).
options.b: When it passes another vessel coming from a direction of more than 22.5° abaft the beam (sector of the masthead light).
options.c: When it approaches another vessel from a direction of more than 22.5° abaft the beam of that vessel (sector of the sternlight).
options.d: When it approaches another vessel from a direction of more than 112.5° abaft the beam of that vessel (sector of the sidelights).

sportboot-see-elwis-81.explanation: A vessel is deemed to be overtaking when it approaches another vessel from a direction more than 22.5° abaft that vessel's beam - i.e. from the sector in which, at night, only that vessel's sternlight would be visible, not either sidelight. In this situation, the overtaking vessel must always keep out of the way, regardless of whether power-driven or sailing vessels are involved.

sportboot-see-elwis-84.question: What special measures must be taken in restricted visibility?

options.a: A safe speed adapted to the reduced visibility must be maintained, sound signals must be given, the radar must be switched on, and a proper lookout must be kept.
options.b: A safe speed adapted to the reduced visibility must be maintained, sound signals must be given, navigation lights must be switched on, and a proper lookout must be kept.
options.c: A safe speed adapted to the reduced visibility must be maintained, sound signals must be given, navigation lights must be switched on, and a radar reflector must be deployed.
options.d: Reduced speed must be maintained, sound signals must be given, navigation lights must be switched on, and AIS (Automatic Identification System) must be switched on.

sportboot-see-elwis-84.explanation: In restricted visibility, every vessel must proceed at a safe speed adapted to the visibility conditions, sound the prescribed fog signals, switch on her navigation lights (even during the day), and keep a proper lookout by sight and hearing and, if fitted, by radar. Radar or AIS alone does not replace these basic obligations.

sportboot-see-elwis-88.question: How must traffic separation schemes be navigated?

options.a: They may only be navigated in one direction within the outer separation lines.
options.b: They may only be navigated in the direction of travel to the left of the separation line or zone.
options.c: They may only be navigated in the general direction of traffic flow to the right of the separation line or zone.
options.d: They may only be navigated from beginning to end, and only in the direction of travel to the right of the separation zone.

sportboot-see-elwis-88.explanation: Each traffic lane of a traffic separation scheme is used only in the general direction of traffic flow prescribed for it, keeping to the right of the separation line or zone - comparable to the right-hand rule of the road on a divided highway. This ensures that opposing traffic travels in separate lanes.

sportboot-see-elwis-90.question: What does "safe speed" mean?

options.a: The speed must be adapted to the traffic situation, the volume of traffic, and the sea and wind conditions, so that no wash or wave action is created.
options.b: The speed must be adapted to the traffic situation, visibility, and weather conditions, and to fuel consumption.
options.c: The speed must be adapted to the traffic situation, visibility, and weather conditions, and traffic must not be obstructed.
options.d: The speed must be adapted to the traffic situation, visibility, and weather conditions, and it must be possible to stop within an appropriate distance at any time.

sportboot-see-elwis-90.explanation: Safe speed means the vessel's speed must be adapted to the traffic situation as well as visibility and weather conditions such that the vessel can, at any time, stop in time or take effective avoiding action to prevent a collision. It is a relative concept dependent on the circumstances at hand, not a fixed numerical value.

sportboot-see-elwis-96.question: What does it mean when every vessel of a tow carries a black diamond shape?

options.a: Tow of more than 50 m in length.
options.b: Tow of less than 50 m in length.
options.c: Tow of more than 200 m in length.
options.d: Tow of more than 100 m in length.

sportboot-see-elwis-96.explanation: When every vessel of a tow (the towing vessel and the vessel(s) being towed) carries a black diamond shape by day, this indicates that the overall length of the tow exceeds 200 m. This warns other traffic to allow sufficient distance and time for avoiding action or overtaking.

sportboot-see-elwis-114.question: What light must a vessel at anchor of less than 50 m in length show?

options.a: A white all-round light where it can best be seen.
options.b: Two red all-round lights where they can best be seen.
options.c: A red all-round light where it can best be seen.
options.d: Two white all-round lights where they can best be seen.

sportboot-see-elwis-114.explanation: A vessel at anchor of less than 50 m in length must show a white all-round light where it can best be seen at night, so that other vessels can recognize her position in time and keep a safe distance.

sportboot-see-elwis-126.question: Two sailing vessels in sight of one another are approaching in the open sea or outside the fairway such that there is a risk of collision. Which vessel must give way to the other if they have the wind on the same side?

options.a: The vessel that is to windward gives way to the vessel that is to leeward.
options.b: The vessel that has the wind on the starboard side.
options.c: The vessel that is to leeward gives way to the vessel that is to windward.
options.d: The vessel that has the wind on the port side.

sportboot-see-elwis-126.explanation: When two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, the windward vessel must give way to the leeward vessel, because the leeward vessel generally has fewer options for bearing away from the wind and adjusting her course.

sportboot-see-elwis-127.question: How must two power-driven vessels in sight of one another behave when approaching on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses, so as to avoid the risk of collision?

options.a: Each vessel must alter her course to port.
options.b: The vessel to leeward must give way to the vessel to windward.
options.c: Each vessel must alter her course to starboard.
options.d: The vessel to windward must give way to the vessel to leeward.

sportboot-see-elwis-127.explanation: When two power-driven vessels are approaching on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses with risk of collision, each must alter course to starboard, so that both vessels pass each other on the port side - comparable to right-hand traffic on the road.

sportboot-see-elwis-128.question: How must a power-driven vessel in the open sea or outside the fairway behave towards a sailing vessel in sight, if there is a risk of collision?

options.a: The power-driven vessel must keep her course and speed.
options.b: The power-driven vessel must give way.
options.c: The power-driven vessel must reduce her speed.
options.d: The power-driven vessel must maneuver cautiously until the danger has passed.

sportboot-see-elwis-128.explanation: In the open sea, a sailing vessel generally ranks above a power-driven vessel in the COLREGs give-way hierarchy, so a power-driven vessel must give way to a sailing vessel when risk of collision exists (sailing vessels typically have more limited maneuvering options, being dependent on the wind).

sportboot-see-elwis-129.question: How must a power-driven vessel in the open sea or outside the fairway behave towards a vessel not under command in sight, if there is a risk of collision?

options.a: The power-driven vessel must alter her course to starboard.
options.b: The power-driven vessel must reduce her speed.
options.c: The power-driven vessel must give way.
options.d: The power-driven vessel must keep her course and speed.

sportboot-see-elwis-129.explanation: Vessels not under command stand at the very top of the give-way hierarchy, since they cannot help themselves; every other vessel - including sailing vessels - must give way to them, and this applies here to the power-driven vessel as well.

sportboot-see-elwis-130.question: How must a power-driven vessel in the open sea or outside the fairway behave towards a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, in sight, if there is a risk of collision?

options.a: The power-driven vessel must alter her course to starboard.
options.b: The power-driven vessel must keep her course and speed.
options.c: The power-driven vessel must give way.
options.d: The power-driven vessel must reduce her speed.

sportboot-see-elwis-130.explanation: Vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver also enjoy special priority because of their limited maneuverability; a power-driven vessel must therefore give way to them, unless the specific nature of the restricted operation requires a different special rule.

sportboot-see-elwis-131.question: How must a power-driven vessel in the open sea or outside the fairway behave towards a vessel engaged in fishing in sight, if there is a risk of collision?

options.a: The power-driven vessel must keep her course and speed.
options.b: The power-driven vessel must give way.
options.c: The power-driven vessel must alter her course to starboard.
options.d: The power-driven vessel must maneuver cautiously until the danger has passed.

sportboot-see-elwis-131.explanation: A vessel whose maneuverability is restricted by fishing with nets, lines, or other gear counts as restricted in her ability to maneuver and ranks above an ordinary power-driven vessel, which must therefore give way to her.

sportboot-see-elwis-132.question: How must a sailing vessel in the open sea or outside the fairway behave towards a vessel engaged in fishing in sight, if there is a risk of collision?

options.a: The sailing vessel must initially keep her course and speed.
options.b: The sailing vessel must give way.
options.c: The sailing vessel must alter her course to starboard.
options.d: The sailing vessel must not impede the safe passage of the vessel.

sportboot-see-elwis-132.explanation: Vessels engaged in fishing rank even above sailing vessels in the COLREGs hierarchy, since their fishing gear severely limits their maneuverability; a sailing vessel must therefore also give way to a vessel engaged in fishing.

sportboot-see-elwis-133.question: What kind of vessel is this and what must be observed?

options.a: Wash and wave action must be avoided.
options.b: The vessel must be passed on the starboard side.
options.c: Course and speed must be kept.
options.d: The safe passage of the vessel must not be impeded.

sportboot-see-elwis-133.explanation: The vessel shown has particularly restricted freedom of movement, for example as a vessel constrained by her draught, which cannot give way because of her draught in relation to the available depth of water. For such vessels there is no ordinary give-way or stand-on duty; instead other vessels have the special duty not to impede her safe passage.

sportboot-see-elwis-134.question: What kind of vessel is this and what must be observed?

options.a: The vessel must be passed on the starboard side.
options.b: Wash and wave action must be avoided.
options.c: The safe passage of the vessel must not be impeded.
options.d: Course and speed must be kept.

sportboot-see-elwis-134.explanation: The vessel shown has restricted freedom of movement, so it cannot simply be fitted into the ordinary give-way rules like a ship maneuvering normally. Other vessels must therefore not impede her safe passage, rather than applying the usual stand-on or give-way duties to her.

sportboot-see-elwis-135.question: How must the stand-on vessel behave towards a give-way vessel before initiating the maneuver of last resort?

options.a: Alter course to starboard, initially keep speed, and pay particular attention to the give-way vessel.
options.b: Initially keep course and speed and pay particular attention to the give-way vessel.
options.c: Alter course to starboard, reduce speed, and pay particular attention to the give-way vessel.
options.d: Adjust course or speed and pay particular attention to the give-way vessel.

sportboot-see-elwis-135.explanation: The stand-on vessel must, for as long as possible, keep course and speed so the give-way vessel can reliably calculate her avoiding action, while paying particular attention to the give-way vessel. Only once it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not reacting appropriately may/must the stand-on vessel intervene herself by carrying out the maneuver of last resort.

sportboot-see-elwis-142.question: What must be observed when using a traffic separation scheme?

options.a: Proceed in the appropriate traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow, keep as far as practicable clear of the separation zone/line, join or leave the lane normally at its end, and if joining or leaving from the side, do so at as small an angle as possible to the general direction of traffic flow.
options.b: Vessels proceeding in the appropriate traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow must keep as far as practicable clear of the separation zone/line and have right of way over all vessels joining or crossing the scheme.
options.c: Proceed in the appropriate traffic lane on the left side of the separation zone in the direction of travel, stay as close as possible to the separation zone/line, join or leave the lane normally at its end, and if joining or leaving from the side, do so at as close as possible to a right angle to the general direction of traffic flow.
options.d: Use of traffic separation schemes is not permitted for sailing vessels or power-driven vessels under 20 m in length. Such vessels must keep as far as practicable clear of traffic separation schemes and must, by their course, make clear they are not using the scheme.

sportboot-see-elwis-142.explanation: Within a traffic separation scheme, proceed in the appropriate traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow, keeping as far as practicable clear of the separation zone or line. Joining or leaving the lane normally happens at its ends; where entering or leaving from the side is necessary, this must be done at as small an angle as possible to the general direction of traffic flow, to disturb through traffic as little as possible.

sportboot-see-elwis-143.question: What must be observed regarding crossing a traffic separation scheme?

options.a: Crossing should be avoided if possible. If crossing is necessary, it must be done with the heading at as acute an angle as possible to the general direction of traffic flow. The heading of the crossing vessel must maintain as acute an angle as possible to the general direction of traffic flow even when the vessel is set off by wind or current.
options.b: Crossing of traffic separation schemes is prohibited for sailing vessels and power-driven vessels under 20 m in length. Such vessels must keep as far as practicable clear of the ends of traffic separation schemes and must, by their course, make clear they are not crossing the scheme.
options.c: Crossing should be avoided if possible. If crossing is necessary, it should be done with the heading as close as possible to a right angle to the general direction of traffic flow. The heading of the crossing vessel must maintain a right angle to the general direction of traffic flow even when the vessel is set off by wind or current.
options.d: Crossing should be avoided if possible. If crossing is necessary, it should be done on a true course as close as possible to the general direction of traffic flow. The true course of the crossing vessel must maintain a right angle to the general direction of traffic flow even when the vessel is set off by wind or current.

sportboot-see-elwis-143.explanation: A vessel that must cross a traffic separation scheme should do so as close as possible to a right angle to the general direction of traffic flow, so as to minimize crossing time and thus the risk to through traffic. This requirement refers to the vessel's actual heading (the course steered), which must be held at a right angle to the traffic direction even when the vessel is being set off course by wind or current - not to the course made good over the ground.

sportboot-see-elwis-146.question: How must a sailing vessel behave, when crossing a traffic separation scheme, towards a power-driven vessel proceeding along a traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow?

options.a: It has right of way. All vessels following the traffic lane must wait.
options.b: It must not impede the safe passage of the power-driven vessel.
options.c: It is bound by the duty to stand on. Course and speed must be kept.
options.d: It must wait. All vessels following the traffic lane have right of way.

sportboot-see-elwis-146.explanation: Vessels crossing a traffic separation scheme - including sailing vessels - must not impede the safe passage of vessels following a traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow. This obligation applies regardless of the otherwise privileged position sailing vessels normally have relative to power-driven vessels.

sportboot-see-elwis-147.question: How must vessels of less than 20 m in length or sailing vessels behave in traffic separation schemes?

options.a: They count as small craft and may not use traffic separation schemes.
options.b: They count as small craft and may only use traffic separation schemes during the day and in good visibility.
options.c: They may use the separation zone, so as not to obstruct through traffic.
options.d: They must not impede the safe passage of a power-driven vessel following the traffic lane.

sportboot-see-elwis-147.explanation: Vessels under 20 m in length and sailing vessels are generally permitted to use traffic separation schemes, but must not impede the safe passage of (typically large, draught-constrained) power-driven vessels proceeding along a traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow, since such vessels have limited ability to give way owing to their size and draught.

sportboot-see-elwis-148.question: What kind of vessel is this and what must be observed?

options.a: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It must not be passed on either side.
options.b: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side that lies on the right relative to my direction of travel.
options.c: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side that shows two black diamonds arranged vertically above one another.
options.d: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side that shows two black balls arranged vertically above one another.

sportboot-see-elwis-148.explanation: The vessel shown is a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver by dredging or underwater operations, obstructing shipping. She shows two black diamond shapes vertically in line (or two green all-round lights at night) on the side on which it is safe to pass, while the obstructed side is marked with two black balls (or two red all-round lights).

sportboot-see-elwis-149.question: What kind of vessel is this and what must be observed?

options.a: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver with way through the water, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side that lies on the left relative to the direction of travel.
options.b: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver with way through the water, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It may be passed on either side.
options.c: A vessel not under command with way through the water, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side that lies on the right relative to the direction of travel.
options.d: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver with way through the water, dredging or engaged in underwater operations but not obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side that lies on the right relative to the direction of travel.

sportboot-see-elwis-149.explanation: If a vessel dredging or conducting underwater operations, despite having way through the water, does not actually obstruct the remaining traffic, no special passing-side signals apply; the normal right-hand traffic rule then governs, meaning she must be passed on the side lying to starboard (the right) relative to the direction of travel.

sportboot-see-elwis-150.question: What kind of vessel is this and what must be observed?

options.a: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver without way through the water, obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side showing two red all-round lights vertically in line.
options.b: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver without way through the water, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the starboard side of the fairway (right-hand traffic rule).
options.c: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver without way through the water, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side showing two green all-round lights vertically in line.
options.d: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver without way through the water, dredging or engaged in underwater operations and obstructing shipping. It must be passed on the side that lies on the left relative to the direction of travel.

sportboot-see-elwis-150.explanation: A vessel that is at anchor or otherwise without way through the water while dredging or conducting underwater operations, and thereby obstructing shipping, shows two green all-round lights vertically in line (two black diamonds by day) on the safe passing side, and two red all-round lights (two black balls by day) on the obstructed side.

sportboot-see-elwis-151.question: What kind of vessel is this and what must be observed?

options.a: Vessel in distress. Render assistance or call for further help.
options.b: Government vessel. It may depart from the traffic rules.
options.c: Vessel with a diver down. Keep a large distance.
options.d: Vessel carrying dangerous goods; keep your distance, smoking and open flame prohibited.

sportboot-see-elwis-151.explanation: Vessels carrying dangerous or hazardous cargo display a special marking (e.g. a red flag "B" or a corresponding all-round light) and, because of the danger of explosion and fire, must only be approached at a sufficient distance; smoking and open flame in their vicinity are strictly prohibited.

sportboot-see-elwis-152.question: Where is it defined which bodies of water are seagoing shipping routes?

options.a: The COLREGs and the Maritime Tasks Act.
options.b: The Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung and the COLREGs.
options.c: The Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung and the Ems Estuary Shipping Regulation.
options.d: The COLREGs and the Ems Estuary Shipping Regulation.

sportboot-see-elwis-152.explanation: Which waters count as seagoing shipping routes is laid down in the annex to the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung and, for the Ems estuary area, in the Schifffahrtsordnung Emsmündung. Both regulations define the geographical scope of the special maritime shipping rules.

sportboot-see-elwis-154.question: What kind of vessel is this and what must be observed?

options.a: A vessel restricted by her draught. It must not be obstructed.
options.b: A German Navy vessel on operations. It carries ammunition or other dangerous goods.
options.c: A government vessel on operations. It may deviate from the traffic rules.
options.d: A pilot vessel with special rights on operations. It may deviate from the right-hand traffic rule.

sportboot-see-elwis-154.explanation: Government-service vessels (e.g. police, customs, water police, rescue services) may, when on operations and identified by appropriate signals, deviate from the general traffic rules to the extent necessary to carry out their official duties - other traffic must leave them sufficient room.

sportboot-see-elwis-158.question: What traffic-law obligation does a skipper have, under section 3 of the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung (SeeSchStrO), if their vessel is equipped with a VHF radio?

options.a: They are required to hold the appropriate radio operator's certificate when using a VHF radio.
options.b: They are required to listen to and take into account the traffic information and assistance broadcast by the traffic center.
options.c: They are required, in restricted visibility, to regularly report their vessel's name and position to the traffic center.
options.d: They are required to keep the radio equipment operating while underway and to log all messages concerning their vessel in the ship's logbook.

sportboot-see-elwis-158.explanation: A skipper operating a vessel fitted with a VHF radio is obliged, under the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung, to listen to the traffic information and assistance broadcast by the relevant traffic center and to take it into account in their navigation, so as to participate in that waterway's traffic management system.

sportboot-see-elwis-163.question: What is the "general danger and warning signal"?

options.a: Two groups of one prolonged and four short blasts each.
options.b: Two groups of three prolonged blasts each.
options.c: Two groups of four short blasts each.
options.d: Two groups of one short and four prolonged blasts each.

sportboot-see-elwis-163.explanation: The general danger and warning signal consists of two groups of one prolonged and four short blasts each, and is used to warn other vessels of an immediate danger when no more specific signal (such as a maneuvering or fog signal) applies.

sportboot-see-elwis-167.question: Which give-way rules apply outside the fairway?

options.a: The rules of the Ems Estuary Shipping Regulation.
options.b: The rules of the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung.
options.c: The rules of the COLREGs.
options.d: The rules of the Binnenschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung.

sportboot-see-elwis-167.explanation: Outside the fairway marked by buoys or beacons, i.e. in the open sea, the general give-way and right-of-way rules of the COLREGs apply, since the fairway-specific rules of the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung (such as the right-hand traffic rule) do not apply there.

sportboot-see-elwis-168.question: Where is overtaking prohibited?

options.a: At narrow passages, blind bends, in lock areas, within stretches marked by overtaking-prohibited signs, near ferries in operation that are not running freely, and outside the fairway.
options.b: At narrow passages, blind bends, within stretches marked by overtaking-prohibited signs, and in national parks and specially designated nature reserves.
options.c: At narrow passages, blind bends, in lock areas, within stretches marked by overtaking-prohibited signs, near ferries in operation that are not running freely, and in traffic separation schemes.
options.d: At narrow passages, blind bends, in lock areas, within stretches marked by overtaking-prohibited signs, and near ferries in operation that are not running freely.

sportboot-see-elwis-168.explanation: Overtaking is generally prohibited at narrow passages, blind bends, in lock approach areas, within stretches marked by overtaking-prohibited signs, and near cable ferries or similar ferries in operation, because in these situations visibility and available space do not allow for a safe overtaking maneuver.

sportboot-see-elwis-170.question: How must operators of tow boats for water-skiers, jet-ski riders, and windsurfers behave when approaching other vessels?

options.a: They must keep course and speed.
options.b: They have right of way and must cross ahead of the other vessel's bow.
options.c: They must stop when approaching other vessels and avoid wash and wave action.
options.d: They must give way.

sportboot-see-elwis-170.explanation: Tow boats for water-skiers, jet-ski riders, and windsurfers are not privileged relative to other vessels; they must always give way when approaching other vessels, since these watersports activities do not grant any special right-of-way status under the give-way rules.

sportboot-see-elwis-172.question: What must be done to warn shipping if your own vessel has sunk and constitutes a navigational hazard?

options.a: You give a distress signal.
options.b: You inform the German Society for the Rescue of Shipwrecked Persons so the hazard can be marked.
options.c: You inform the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency and give the position if possible.
options.d: You inform the shipping police authority and give the position if possible.

sportboot-see-elwis-172.explanation: If your own sunken vessel constitutes a hazard to navigation, the competent shipping police authority must be informed so that the hazard can be marked and other vessels warned; the exact position should be provided if possible.

sportboot-see-elwis-174.question: Where can rules for transiting the Kiel Canal (NOK) be found?

options.a: Supplementary provisions for the NOK in the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung, as well as in the Sportbootführerscheinverordnung.
options.b: Supplementary provisions for the NOK in the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung, as well as in the COLREGs.
options.c: Supplementary provisions for the NOK in the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung, as well as in the Maritime Tasks Act.
options.d: Supplementary provisions for the NOK in the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung, as well as in the notices of the Generaldirektion Wasserstraßen und Schifffahrt (GDWS).

sportboot-see-elwis-174.explanation: In addition to the Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung, the notices issued by the Generaldirektion Wasserstraßen und Schifffahrt (GDWS) contain the specific rules for transiting the Kiel Canal (Nord-Ostsee-Kanal), such as reporting duties, speed, and behavior in the locks.

sportboot-see-elwis-183.question: How can you recognize a military warning area that is closed to shipping because of firing exercises?

options.a: By specific day and night signals which, under the Sperr- und Warngebietsverordnung of the Generaldirektion Wasserstraßen und Schifffahrt (GDWS) for military restricted and warning areas, are shown at designated signal stations and on safety vessels.
options.b: By specific day and night signals which, under the applicable police regulation of the water management authority for exercise, restricted, and warning areas, are shown at designated signal stations on shore and on safety vessels.
options.c: By specific day and night signals which, under the shipping regulation of the Generaldirektion Wasserstraßen und Schifffahrt (GDWS) for military restricted and warning areas, are shown at designated signal stations on shore and on safety vessels.
options.d: By specific day and night signals which, under the Rhine police regulation of the Generaldirektion Wasserstraßen und Schifffahrt (GDWS) for military restricted and warning areas, are shown at designated signal stations on shore and on safety vessels.

sportboot-see-elwis-183.explanation: Military restricted and warning areas closed to shipping because of firing exercises are indicated by specific day and night signals, laid down in the GDWS's Sperr- und Warngebietsverordnung for military restricted and warning areas, shown at designated signal stations and on safety vessels, so that boaters can recognize the closure in good time.

sportboot-see-elwis-197.question: What does the following light characteristic mean: "Oc (2) R. Whis."?

options.a: Flashing (2) red, bell buoy.
options.b: Quick flashing (2) red, bell buoy.
options.c: Occulting (2) red, whistle buoy.
options.d: Red leading light, two warning sectors.

sportboot-see-elwis-197.explanation: In the international buoyage and light characteristic notation, "Oc" stands for "occulting" (a light that is mostly on, with brief eclipses), the "(2)" indicates a group of two eclipses per period, "R" denotes the color red, and "Whis." indicates a whistle sound signal - together describing a red buoy with an occulting group-two light and a whistle.

sportboot-see-elwis-198.question: What light characteristic and color do the lighted buoys on the starboard side of the fairway have?

options.a: Green flashing light, quick flashing light, or occulting light in groups.
options.b: Green flashing light, quick flashing light, or fixed light.
options.c: Green flashing light, quick flashing light, or single flashing light.
options.d: Green flashing light, quick flashing light, or very quick flashing light.

sportboot-see-elwis-198.explanation: Lighted buoys on the starboard side of the fairway (conical, green buoys in the IALA Region A system) show a green light, which may be characterized as a flashing light, a quick flashing light, or an occulting light shown in groups. The color green, in Germany (Region A), marks the starboard side of the channel when proceeding inbound (from sea towards harbor).

sportboot-see-elwis-199.question: What colour and light characteristic do the lit buoys on the port side of the fairway show?

options.a: Red flashing light, sparkling light or occulting light.
options.b: Red flashing light, sparkling light or group-interrupted light.
options.c: Red flashing light, sparkling light or fixed light.
options.d: Red flashing light, sparkling light or quick-sparkling light.

sportboot-see-elwis-199.explanation: Port-hand buoys and their lit versions show a red light. Under the internationally used IALA buoyage system (Region A), this red light can be shown as a flashing light, a sparkling light, or a group-interrupted (grouped) light, but not as a simple occulting light. The exact light characteristic is shown on nautical charts and in the list of lights and is used to unambiguously identify which side of the channel the mark is on at night.

sportboot-see-elwis-211.question: How does a leading (directional) light get used for navigation?

options.a: Keep to the left side of the white sector, in the direction of travel.
options.b: Keep to the right side of the white sector, in the direction of travel.
options.c: Keep the upper and lower lights in transit (in line), in the direction of travel.
options.d: Keep in the middle of the white sector, in the direction of travel.

sportboot-see-elwis-211.explanation: A directional light produces a white sector marking the safe course along a fairway, usually flanked by red and green sectors marking the danger areas on the left and right (red = port side, green = starboard side of the direction of travel). Since traffic normally keeps to the right, a boat navigates by keeping to the right (green) side of the white sector in the direction of travel, staying in the safe channel and giving way to oncoming traffic.

sportboot-see-elwis-214.question: How does a lateral (transverse) light get used for navigation?

options.a: Alter course at the transition from the warning sector into the course-change sector.
options.b: Keep the upper and lower lights in transit (in line) on reaching the warning sector.
options.c: Alter course on reaching the warning sector.
options.d: Maintain course on reaching the course-change sector.

sportboot-see-elwis-214.explanation: A transverse (cross) light marks an upcoming change of course in the fairway by means of different sectors: a warning sector that signals the approaching course change, and a course-change sector in which the alteration is actually to be carried out. At the transition from the warning sector into the course-change sector, the boat steers onto the new course, so the vessel follows the fairway's bend in good time and under control.

sportboot-see-elwis-215.question: What is meant by an occulting light?

options.a: The light phase is always equal in length to the dark phase.
options.b: The light phase is always shorter than 2 seconds.
options.c: The light phase is always shorter than the dark phase.
options.d: The light phase is always longer than the dark phase.

sportboot-see-elwis-215.explanation: An occulting light is characterised by the light phase (illumination) always lasting longer than the dark phase (eclipse) between flashes. This distinguishes it from other characteristics such as flashing lights, where the light phase is shorter than the dark phase. Such characteristics allow lights to be unambiguously identified on charts and in lists of lights.

sportboot-see-elwis-216.question: Where can you find the boundaries of nature reserves at sea?

options.a: On the nautical charts and recreational boating charts of the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH).
options.b: In the Maritime Traffic Regulations (Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung).
options.c: In the Federal Nature Conservation Act.
options.d: In the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.

sportboot-see-elwis-216.explanation: The exact boundaries of marine nature reserves are marked on official nautical charts and the special recreational boating charts published by the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH). These charts must be consulted during voyage planning so that skippers can recognise protected areas and comply with the navigation restrictions that apply there.

sportboot-see-elwis-217.question: Where can excerpts of information on navigation restrictions in nature reserves in coastal waters be found?

options.a: In the Maritime Traffic Regulations (Seeschifffahrtsstraßen-Ordnung).
options.b: In the Federal Nature Conservation Act.
options.c: On the nautical charts and recreational boating charts of the Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH).
options.d: In the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.

sportboot-see-elwis-217.explanation: Besides the boundaries of nature reserves, the BSH's nautical charts and recreational boating charts also print excerpts of the navigation restrictions that apply there, such as closed zones, permitted corridors, or speed limits. These chart notes do not replace the full legal ordinances, but give skippers the key practical information needed for the voyage.

sportboot-see-elwis-218.question: Why should approaching seal banks in the Wadden Sea area be avoided?

options.a: So the animals are not disturbed or driven away.
options.b: Seal banks are closed water areas.
options.c: Shallow water must be expected in the area of seal banks.
options.d: Depth information for seal banks is not shown on the charts.

sportboot-see-elwis-218.explanation: Seals rest and nurse their pups on sandbanks that fall dry in the Wadden Sea. Approaching too closely with a boat startles the animals, causing them to flee into the water in panic, which is especially dangerous and energy-draining for pups. For reasons of animal and nature protection, seal banks should therefore be given a wide berth.

sportboot-see-elwis-219.question: According to the '10 golden rules' for the behaviour of watersports enthusiasts, what minimum distance should be kept from seal haul-out sites and bird gatherings?
sportboot-see-elwis-219.explanation: According to the '10 golden rules' for watersports enthusiasts in the Wadden Sea, a minimum distance of 300 m to 500 m should be kept from seal haul-out sites and bird gatherings. This generous distance is meant to prevent the animals from being disturbed or startled into flight by noise, boat movement, or the approach of the vessel.

sportboot-see-elwis-220.question: What is meant by a flashing light?

options.a: Light phase longer than dark phase, flash less than 2 s.
options.b: Light phase shorter than dark phase, flash less than 2 s.
options.c: Light phase shorter than dark phase, flash at least 2 s.
options.d: Light phase longer than dark phase, flash at least 2 s.

sportboot-see-elwis-220.explanation: A flashing light is characterised by brief flashes of light that are always shorter than the dark phase between them, with each individual flash lasting at least 2 seconds. This distinguishes it from a quick-flashing (blitz) light, where the light phase is also shorter than the dark phase but each flash lasts less than 2 seconds.

sportboot-see-elwis-221.question: What is meant by a quick-flashing (blitz) light?

options.a: Light phase longer than dark phase, flash less than 2 s.
options.b: Light phase shorter than dark phase, flash less than 2 s.
options.c: Light phase shorter than dark phase, flash longer than 2 s.
options.d: Light phase longer than dark phase, flash at least 2 s.

sportboot-see-elwis-221.explanation: A quick-flashing (blitz) light shows light phases that are shorter than the dark phase, with each individual flash lasting less than 2 seconds. This distinguishes it from a flashing light, whose light phase is also shorter than the dark phase but lasts at least 2 seconds. This distinction matters for identifying lights unambiguously by their characteristic.

sportboot-see-elwis-222.question: What is meant by a sparkling (very quick) light?

options.a: 100 to 120 consecutive flashes per minute.
options.b: 30 to 40 consecutive flashes per minute.
options.c: 50 to 60 consecutive flashes per minute.
options.d: 130 to 150 consecutive flashes per minute.

sportboot-see-elwis-222.explanation: A sparkling (very quick) light is characterised by a very high frequency of 50 to 60 consecutive flashes per minute. It is often used where a particularly conspicuous, rapidly pulsing characteristic is needed, for example on important fairway marks, so it stands out clearly from slower characteristics such as flashing or quick-flashing lights.

sportboot-see-elwis-223.question: What is meant by an isophase light?

options.a: Light phase longer than dark phase.
options.b: Light phase twice as long as the dark phase.
options.c: Light phase shorter than dark phase.
options.d: Light and dark phases of equal length.

sportboot-see-elwis-223.explanation: An isophase light is characterised by the light phase and the dark phase being of equal length, so the light shines and is dark for the same duration in a regular alternation. This particular characteristic is distinct from fixed, flashing, quick-flashing, and sparkling lights, where the light and dark phases differ in length.

sportboot-see-elwis-224.question: What is meant by the period of a light?

options.a: The time from the start of one occurrence of the light's characteristic to the start of the next identical occurrence.
options.b: The time from the start of the characteristic to the end of that same characteristic.
options.c: The time from the end of the characteristic to the start of the next identical characteristic.
options.d: The time from the start of the characteristic to the end of the next identical characteristic.

sportboot-see-elwis-224.explanation: The period of a light is the time from the start of one occurrence of its characteristic pattern to the start of the next identical occurrence — i.e. the full duration of the repeating light cycle. It is given in seconds on charts and in lists of lights, and together with the type of characteristic allows a light to be identified unambiguously.

sportboot-see-elwis-225.question: How should you behave when navigating through nature reserves and national parks?

options.a: Comply with navigation regulations and the orders of the local regulatory authorities.
options.b: Comply with navigation regulations and inform the water police and the waterways and shipping office.
options.c: Comply with navigation regulations and register with the national park administration.
options.d: Comply with navigation regulations.

sportboot-see-elwis-225.explanation: When navigating through nature reserves and national parks, only the applicable navigation regulations (e.g. under the relevant ordinances) need to be observed; no additional registration or notification to authorities is generally required.
