These regulations set out where, when, and at what speed boats may travel in order to preserve the protective purpose of the area.

sportboot-see-elwis-226.question: What special provisions do the local navigation regulations in nature reserves and national parks contain?

options.a: Navigation bans, meteorological restrictions, special rules for navigating deep-water zones.
options.b: Navigation bans, navigation restrictions, speed limits, special rules for water-skiing, jet-skiing, and windsurfing.
options.c: Navigation bans, navigation restrictions, minimum speeds, special rules for navigating traffic separation zones.
options.d: Navigation bans, shipping closures, speed limits, special rules for navigating wind farms.

sportboot-see-elwis-226.explanation: Local navigation regulations in nature reserves and national parks in particular contain navigation bans and restrictions for certain zones, speed limits, and special rules for activities with high disturbance potential such as water-skiing, jet-skiing, and windsurfing. These rules are meant to protect sensitive wildlife and plant life from excessive disturbance.

sportboot-see-elwis-227.question: What kinds of traffic can be permitted in a designated permission zone?

options.a: Certain equipment for the exploration of fossil fuels.
options.b: Certain watersports equipment.
options.c: Certain fishing vessels.
options.d: Certain ground-effect and hovercraft vehicles.

sportboot-see-elwis-227.explanation: In designated permission zones within protected areas, certain watersports equipment, such as kitesurfing or windsurfing gear, may be permitted under specified conditions. This allows a controlled balance between watersports enthusiasts' recreational interests and the protective purpose of the area.

sportboot-see-elwis-228.question: According to the North Sea Navigation Ordinance (NordSBefV), what is meant by 'fast lane corridors'?

options.a: Designated water areas for certain recreational boat traffic.
options.b: Designated water areas for commercial traffic.
options.c: Water areas from which divers must keep a distance of 500 m.
options.d: Water areas for seaplanes to take off and land.

sportboot-see-elwis-228.explanation: Under the North Sea Navigation Ordinance (NordSBefV), fast lane corridors are designated water areas in which commercial traffic (e.g. passenger vessels, transport to offshore installations) is permitted to travel at increased speed through otherwise protected or speed-restricted areas. This accommodates the commercial need for swift passage while the remaining protected-area regulations continue to apply.

sportboot-see-elwis-230.question: What obligation does a skipper have to help keep waters clean?

options.a: Discharge wastewater near shore, near beaches, and in harbours.
options.b: Dispose of only biodegradable waste and empty containers at sea.
options.c: Collect all waste, including oils and operating fluids, on board in suitable containers and dispose of it properly ashore.
options.d: Dispose of waste and oils only on the open sea.

sportboot-see-elwis-230.explanation: To protect marine and coastal waters, every skipper is obliged to collect all waste generated on board, including used oil and spent operating fluids, in suitable containers and to dispose of it properly only ashore at designated disposal facilities. Discharging or disposing of waste on the water, even on the open sea, is generally not permitted.

sportboot-see-elwis-231.question: Which official nautical publications provide information about the intended cruising area?

options.a: Nautical charts, the Ordinance on the Safety of Maritime Navigation, sailing directions, tide tables or tidal calendars, the radio service for small craft and yachting, Notices to Mariners (NfS).
options.b: Shipping police orders, tide tables or the radio service for small craft and yachting, Notices to Mariners (NfS), Announcements for Mariners (BfS).
options.c: Maritime Traffic Regulations, list of lights, sailing directions, the Ordinance on the Safety of Maritime Navigation, tide tables or tidal calendars, announcements of the Directorate-General for Waterways and Shipping (GDWS).
options.d: Nautical charts, list of lights, sailing directions, tide tables or tidal calendars, the radio service for small craft and yachting, Notices to Mariners (NfS), Announcements for Mariners (BfS).

sportboot-see-elwis-231.explanation: Several official nautical publications provide information about a given cruising area: nautical charts and lists of lights show navigational aids and hazards, sailing directions (Seehandbücher) give detailed descriptions of the area, tide tables or tidal calendars give information on tides, and the radio service for small craft and yachting together with Notices to Mariners (NfS) and Announcements for Mariners (BfS) provide up-to-date information on changes and hazards.

sportboot-see-elwis-236.question: In what units of measurement are depths given on German nautical charts?

options.a: In metres and decimetres.
options.b: In metres and centimetres.
options.c: In decimetres and centimetres.
options.d: In feet and inches.

sportboot-see-elwis-236.explanation: On German nautical charts, water depths are given in metres and decimetres (e.g. 3.5 m corresponds to 3 m 5 dm), as this precision is sufficient for safe navigation and assessing draught. Other units such as feet and inches are mainly used on Anglo-Saxon or older charts.

sportboot-see-elwis-237.question: Where can you find the meanings and explanations of symbols, abbreviations, and terms used on German nautical charts?

options.a: In the INT1 chart (Chart No. 1).
options.b: In the lists of lights.
options.c: In the bottom left corner of every nautical chart.
options.d: In the sailing directions (Seehandbücher).

sportboot-see-elwis-237.explanation: The meanings and explanations of all symbols, abbreviations, and terms used on German nautical charts are compiled in the so-called INT1 (Chart No. 1). It serves as a reference to correctly read and interpret symbols for buoys, lights, hazards, seabed types, and so on.

sportboot-see-elwis-245.question: What is meant by 'set' (current drift)?

options.a: The displacement of the vessel through the water, in direction and distance.
options.b: The direction and strength of the ocean current.
options.c: The deviation of the vessel from the magnetic compass course.
options.d: The displacement of the vessel over ground, in direction and distance.

sportboot-see-elwis-245.explanation: 'Set' (current drift, Stromversetzung) refers to the deviation of a vessel's actual track over the ground from its steered course, caused by water current, expressed in direction and distance. It must be taken into account together with leeway when navigating, in order to correctly determine the vessel's actual position and course over ground (dead reckoning).

sportboot-see-elwis-246.question: What is meant by 'leeway'?

options.a: The displacement of the vessel over ground, in direction and distance.
options.b: The displacement of the vessel through the water, in direction and distance.
options.c: The deviation of the vessel from the magnetic compass course.
options.d: The direction and strength of the wind and wind-driven sea.

sportboot-see-elwis-246.explanation: Leeway (Windversetzung) refers to the deviation of a vessel's actual track over the ground from its steered course caused by the effect of wind, expressed in direction and distance. It arises because wind and wind-driven sea push the boat sideways off the steered course, and must be taken into account together with current set when navigating.

sportboot-see-elwis-248.question: What must be considered when installing a magnetic compass on board?

options.a: The compass must run parallel to the keel line. The compass must have clearly legible figures and must not be installed near iron parts.
options.b: The lubber's line must run parallel to the keel line. The compass must be easily readable and must not be installed near iron parts.
options.c: The lubber's line must run parallel to the keel line. The compass must have clearly legible figures and must not be installed near iron parts.
options.d: The compass must run parallel to the keel line. The compass must be easily readable and must not be installed near iron parts.

sportboot-see-elwis-248.explanation: When installing a magnetic compass on board, the lubber's line (the reference mark) must be aligned exactly parallel to the boat's keel line so that the course read off matches the boat's actual heading. In addition, the compass must be easily readable and installed at a sufficient distance from iron parts and other sources of magnetic interference to avoid deviation errors.

sportboot-see-elwis-257.question: What must be observed when a sportboat is to be towed?

options.a: The tow line must be adjusted to the sea state. Towing speed must not exceed the speed the towing vessel could reach on its own, running free in displacement mode. A sudden jerking as the line comes taut must be avoided.
options.b: The tow line must be adjusted to the weather conditions. Towing speed must not exceed the speed the towing vessel could reach on its own, running free on the plane. A sudden jerking as the line comes taut must be avoided.
options.c: The tow line must be adjusted to the weather conditions. Towing speed must not exceed the speed the towed vessel could reach on its own, running free on the plane. A sudden jerking as the line comes taut must be avoided.
options.d: The tow line must be adjusted to the sea state. Towing speed must not exceed the speed the towed vessel could reach on its own, running free in displacement mode. A sudden jerking as the line comes taut must be avoided.

sportboot-see-elwis-257.explanation: When towing a sportboat, the length of the tow line must be matched to the prevailing sea state so it is not too short and does not part or endanger the towed boat. Towing speed must not exceed the speed the towed vessel (the tow) could achieve on its own in displacement mode, and sudden jerking as the line comes taut (shock loading) must be avoided by anticipatory handling of the boat.

sportboot-see-elwis-258.question: What can be used to keep a disabled sportboat head-to-wind?

options.a: With a drogue deployed both forward and aft, or other suitable buoyant objects.
options.b: By repeatedly briefly engaging and disengaging the propulsion engine.
options.c: With a drogue deployed aft, or similar buoyant objects.
options.d: With a drogue or other suitable buoyant objects.

sportboot-see-elwis-258.explanation: A disabled sportboat can be turned and held head-to-wind with the help of a drogue (sea anchor) or other suitable buoyant objects. The drogue is deployed from the bow and creates water resistance, causing the boat to align itself automatically bow-on into wind and sea, which reduces the risk of capsizing and makes staying on board safer.

sportboot-see-elwis-262.question: How are points of equal air pressure shown on a weather chart, and in what unit is air pressure given?

options.a: By isoclines, in decipascals.
options.b: By isobars, in hectopascals.
options.c: By isoclines, in hectopascals.
options.d: By isobars, in millipascals.

sportboot-see-elwis-262.explanation: Points of equal air pressure are shown on weather charts by isobars, lines connecting points of equal pressure. Air pressure itself is given in hectopascals (hPa); isobars packed closely together indicate a steep pressure gradient and therefore stronger winds.

sportboot-see-elwis-265.question: What does the following illustration show?

options.a: A high-pressure system in the southern hemisphere, isobars with air pressure given in hPa, moving southwest.
options.b: A high-pressure system in the southern hemisphere, isobars with air pressure given in hPa.
options.c: A high-pressure system in the northern hemisphere, isobars with air pressure given in hPa.
options.d: A high-pressure system in the northern hemisphere, isobars with air pressure given in hPa, moving northwest.

sportboot-see-elwis-265.explanation: In the northern hemisphere, wind circulates clockwise around a high-pressure system and flows outward from its centre, which can be recognised on a weather chart from the arrangement and course of the isobars with air pressure given in hPa. This direction of circulation is reversed on the southern hemisphere, where the rotation around high- and low-pressure systems is opposite.

sportboot-see-elwis-270.question: What do the terms 'severe storm', 'violent storm', and 'hurricane force' mean in official weather reports?

options.a: Wind forces 10, 11, and 12 on the Beaufort scale.
options.b: Wind forces 8, 9, and 10 on the Beaufort scale.
options.c: Wind forces 9, 10, and 11 on the Beaufort scale.
options.d: Wind forces 11, 12, and 13 on the Beaufort scale.

sportboot-see-elwis-270.explanation: In official weather reports, the terms 'severe storm', 'violent storm', and 'hurricane force' correspond to wind forces 10, 11, and 12 on the Beaufort scale. This classification lets watersports enthusiasts immediately infer the expected wind strength and the associated hazard from the weather report.

sportboot-see-elwis-272.question: What is the primary purpose of the Automatic Identification System (AIS)?

options.a: Transmitting nautical warning messages.
options.b: Determining position.
options.c: Receiving weather data.
options.d: Collision avoidance.

sportboot-see-elwis-272.explanation: The Automatic Identification System (AIS) primarily serves collision avoidance by allowing vessels to automatically exchange position, course, speed, and other data by radio and display it on screen. This lets other traffic participants and vessel traffic services recognise ship movements early and take appropriate avoiding action in good time.

sportboot-see-elwis-273.question: What kind of information can be exchanged via the Automatic Identification System (AIS)?

options.a: Ship data (static and dynamic), weather data.
options.b: Ship data (static), voyage-related data.
options.c: Ship data (dynamic), weather data.
options.d: Ship data (static and dynamic), voyage-related data.

sportboot-see-elwis-273.explanation: AIS automatically exchanges both static ship data (e.g. name, call sign, ship type, dimensions) and dynamic ship data (position, course, speed), as well as voyage-related data (e.g. destination port, estimated time of arrival, draught) between vessels and vessel traffic services. This comprehensive information supports traffic monitoring and collision avoidance.

sportboot-see-elwis-274.question: Beyond the conduct required by the collision regulations, what safety measures should be taken on board in restricted visibility as a matter of good seamanship?

options.a: In particular, use all navigational equipment carefully, increase the visibility of one's own vessel (e.g. radar reflector, AIS), and continuously keep the vessel traffic service informed of course and speed.
options.b: In particular, use all navigational equipment carefully, increase the visibility of one's own vessel (e.g. radar reflector, AIS), and, in an area with shore-based radar assistance, monitor the radar guidance broadcast over VHF radio.
options.c: In particular, switch on all technical equipment, e.g. radar, echo sounder, AIS, autopilot, and continuously keep the vessel traffic service informed of course and speed.
options.d: In particular, switch on all technical equipment, e.g. radar, AIS, echo sounder, autopilot, and, in an area with shore-based radar assistance, request the radar guidance over VHF radio.

sportboot-see-elwis-274.explanation: Beyond the conduct prescribed by the collision regulations for restricted visibility, good seamanship requires the careful use of all available navigation equipment and increasing your own vessel's visibility to others, for example by rigging a radar reflector or using AIS. In areas with shore-based radar assistance, you should also monitor the radar guidance broadcast over VHF radio to gain additional traffic information.

sportboot-see-elwis-276.question: What aids can be used to quickly and safely bring a person overboard back on deck?

options.a: Line connection, bathing ladder, drogue, rescue sling, lifting net, tackle.
options.b: Line connection, rescue sling, lifting net, tackle, bathing ladder, boom.
options.c: Line connection, boom, anchor chain, tackle, bathing ladder, rescue sling.
options.d: Line connection, bathing ladder, rescue buoy, lifting net, boom, tackle.

sportboot-see-elwis-276.explanation: Several aids are suited for quickly and safely recovering a person floating in the water: a line to pull the person alongside, a rescue sling or lifting net to secure them, a tackle for mechanical assistance in hoisting, a bathing ladder to climb up, and, where available, the boom as a lifting device. These means allow the person to be brought safely back aboard even when the remaining crew has limited physical strength.

sportboot-see-elwis-277.question: What should you do if the vessel has capsized?

options.a: Stay with the vessel if possible and send distress signals. Keep the crew together and avoid unnecessary exertion.
options.b: Stay with the vessel if possible and mark the accident site; avoid unnecessary exertion and attract attention to obtain help.
options.c: Stay with the vessel if possible and keep the crew together; avoid unnecessary exertion and attract attention to obtain help.
options.d: Stay with the vessel if possible and keep the crew together; recover valuables and the ship's log.

sportboot-see-elwis-277.explanation: If a vessel has capsized, the crew should stay with it as far as possible, since even capsized it usually still provides buoyancy and is easier to spot than individuals in the water. The crew should stay together, avoid unnecessary exertion (for instance by swimming against wind and current), and actively draw attention to themselves to summon help.

sportboot-see-elwis-281.question: What does a continuous sound signal from a fog signalling device on a vessel mean?

options.a: Vessel in distress.
options.b: Warning signal.
options.c: Keep-away signal.
options.d: Vessel carrying dangerous goods.

sportboot-see-elwis-281.explanation: A continuous sounding of a fog signalling device (as opposed to short blasts or specific signal sequences) is, under the collision regulations, a distress signal from a vessel in distress. It must be clearly distinguished from other signals such as a warning signal or manoeuvring signals, so it is immediately recognised and correctly interpreted in an emergency.

sportboot-see-elwis-283.question: What does a rocket parachute flare showing a red star mean?

options.a: Distress.
options.b: Request to alter course.
options.c: Request to stop.
options.d: Firing/shooting exercise.

sportboot-see-elwis-283.explanation: A rocket flare showing red stars is an internationally recognised pyrotechnic distress signal. It is used to draw attention to a person or vessel in distress and to summon help, and must be clearly distinguished from other signals (e.g. white signal flares used for manoeuvring purposes).

sportboot-see-elwis-89.question: What does 'in sight of one another' mean?

options.a: When every vessel can be visually observed even in poor visibility conditions.
options.b: When both vessels can be visually observed.
options.c: When each skipper can be visually observed by the other.
options.d: When each vessel can be visually observed from the other.

sportboot-see-elwis-89.explanation: 'In sight of one another' under the collision regulations means that two vessels can visually observe each other, i.e. can be seen with the naked eye and not just detected by radar. Only when this condition is met do the give-way rules for vessels in sight of one another apply; when a vessel is detected only by radar (e.g. in fog), the special rules for restricted visibility apply instead.

sportboot-see-elwis-256.question: How long should a tow line be in heavy seas?

options.a: At least two to three times the wave length.
options.b: At least two to three times the wave height.
options.c: At least two to three times the vessel length.
options.d: At least two to three times the water depth.

sportboot-see-elwis-256.explanation: In heavy seas, the tow line should be at least two to three times the wave length. This ideally keeps the towing vessel and the towed vessel simultaneously in a wave trough or on a wave crest together, preventing sudden jerking loads and the line parting.

sportboot-see-elwis-259.question: Why should speed be reduced in heavy seas?

options.a: To avoid damage from pounding (slamming).
options.b: To avoid the vessel's length coming into resonance with the wave length.
options.c: To minimise pitching and rolling motions.
options.d: To avoid the propeller breaking the surface and to save fuel.

sportboot-see-elwis-259.explanation: In heavy seas, speed should be reduced to avoid damage from pounding (slamming), i.e. the hull striking the waves hard at excessive speed. Reduced speed protects the hull structure, lowers the strain on crew and equipment, and improves the vessel's controllability in a seaway.

sportboot-see-elwis-263.question: What must be expected when air pressure is falling rapidly?

options.a: A deterioration in the weather.
options.b: An improvement in the weather.
options.c: Light winds or calm conditions.
options.d: Strong winds or storm conditions.

sportboot-see-elwis-263.explanation: A rapidly falling air pressure indicates an approaching low-pressure system or an active frontal zone and is a reliable warning sign of oncoming strong winds or a storm. Skippers should therefore treat a rapid pressure drop as a cue to seek shelter or take safety precautions in good time.

sportboot-see-elwis-264.question: What do the isobars shown on a weather chart mean?

options.a: Points of equal air pressure.
options.b: Points of equal cloud formation.
options.c: Points of equal wind strength.
options.d: Points of equal humidity.

sportboot-see-elwis-264.explanation: Isobars on a weather chart connect points of equal air pressure. Their spacing indicates the pressure gradient: closely spaced isobars mean a steep gradient and therefore stronger winds, while widely spaced isobars indicate weaker winds.

sportboot-see-elwis-266.question: What does the following illustration show?

options.a: A low-pressure system in the southern hemisphere with a warm front ahead of the cold front, air pressure given in hPa, showing warm and cold air currents.
options.b: A low-pressure system in the northern hemisphere with a cold front ahead of the warm front, air pressure given in hPa, warm front south, cold front north of the centre.
options.c: A low-pressure system in the southern hemisphere with a warm and a cold front, isobars with air pressure given in hPa, cold and warm air currents.
options.d: A low-pressure system in the northern hemisphere with a warm and a cold front, isobars with air pressure given in hPa, warm and cold air currents.

sportboot-see-elwis-266.explanation: In the northern hemisphere, a low-pressure system typically has its warm front leading (in the direction of travel) with the cold front following behind; the isobars show air pressure in hPa, and arrows or symbols indicate the warm and cold air currents. This pattern is characteristic of extratropical lows in the northern hemisphere and differs in circulation direction from lows in the southern hemisphere.

sportboot-see-elwis-267.question: For what wind forces is a strong wind warning issued?

options.a: Wind force 6 and 7 on the Beaufort scale.
options.b: Wind force 4 to 5 on the Beaufort scale.
options.c: Wind force 7 to 8 on the Beaufort scale.
options.d: Wind force 5 and 6 on the Beaufort scale.

sportboot-see-elwis-267.explanation: A strong wind warning is issued for wind forces 6 and 7 on the Beaufort scale, i.e. a strong to near-gale breeze. It is meant to alert watersports enthusiasts early to increasingly rough conditions, under which putting to sea in a small sportboat can become risky.

sportboot-see-elwis-268.question: For what wind forces is a gale warning issued?

options.a: Wind force 9 and above on the Beaufort scale.
options.b: Wind force 6 and above on the Beaufort scale.
options.c: Wind force 7 and above on the Beaufort scale.
options.d: Wind force 8 and above on the Beaufort scale.

sportboot-see-elwis-268.explanation: A gale warning is issued for wind force 8 and above on the Beaufort scale. From this wind force onward, considerably rough seas, streaks of foam, and severely limited handling of small sportboats must be expected, so shelter should be sought in good time.

sportboot-see-elwis-269.question: What is meant by 'fresh breeze' in official weather reports?

options.a: Wind force 7 on the Beaufort scale.
options.b: Wind force 4 on the Beaufort scale.
options.c: Wind force 5 on the Beaufort scale.
options.d: Wind force 6 on the Beaufort scale.

sportboot-see-elwis-269.explanation: In official weather reports, the term 'fresh breeze' corresponds to wind force 5 on the Beaufort scale. This wind strength already produces noticeably choppy seas with white foam crests and calls for corresponding caution when handling small sportboats.

sportboot-see-elwis-275.question: What safety measures should be taken at sea before the onset of severe weather (strong wind, storm)?

options.a: Secure the vessel in a watertight condition, lash down loose objects, put on life jackets and have other life-saving equipment ready; if necessary and possible, head for a port of refuge.
options.b: Secure the vessel in a watertight condition, lash down loose objects, have life jackets and other life-saving equipment ready, prepare distress signalling equipment for use.
options.c: Close doors, lash down loose objects, have life jackets and other life-saving equipment ready, man radar, helm, and VHF.
options.d: Close doors, lash down loose objects, have life jackets and other life-saving equipment ready, prepare distress signalling equipment for use.

sportboot-see-elwis-275.explanation: Before severe weather (strong wind, storm) sets in at sea, preventive safety measures must be taken: securing the vessel watertight (closing hatches, doors, companionways), lashing down loose objects on deck and below, putting on life jackets, and keeping other life-saving equipment ready. If necessary and possible, a port of refuge should be reached in good time to avoid the severe weather.

sportboot-see-elwis-278.question: How can persons falling overboard in heavy seas be prevented?

options.a: Flake out safety lines or harness tethers, put on a safety harness, and clip onto the guardrail.
options.b: Tension safety lines or harnesses, gather the crew on deck, put on life jackets.
options.c: Gather the crew in the cockpit, put on life jackets, tension safety lines or harnesses.
options.d: Tension safety lines or harnesses, put on a safety harness, and clip on at the designated attachment points.

sportboot-see-elwis-278.explanation: To prevent persons from falling overboard in heavy seas, safety lines or jacklines should be rigged taut between suitable fixed points. Each person should then put on a safety harness and clip on at the designated attachment points, so they remain secured on deck even when the boat moves violently.
